mediate

MEE-dee-ayt -- three syllables, stress on the first syllable, MEE. Don't confuse it with 'meditate,' which has a T and means to reflect quietly. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To mediate is to intervene between two parties in a dispute and help them reach their own agreement.

The city hired a professional to mediate between the developers and the neighborhood association.

Example

Two roommates haven't spoken in a week over the mess in the kitchen, so a third friend offers to mediate: she sits them both down, hears each side, and helps them write a chore schedule they can both accept.

To mediate is to step in between the two sides as a neutral helper and guide them to their own agreement -- to intervene between parties in conflict, never to take a side.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

intercede: To intercede is to step in on one person's behalf -- you plead your friend's case with the angry coach. To mediate is to stay strictly in the middle. Someone who intercedes takes a side and argues for it; a mediator favors neither side and helps both reach their own agreement.

reconcile: To reconcile is to bring people back into friendly relations after a falling-out -- it names the happy result. To mediate is the work in the middle: a neutral helper guiding both sides toward their own agreement. You mediate the dispute; if it succeeds, the former enemies reconcile.

broker: To broker is to arrange a deal between parties -- a broker wants the agreement signed and may push both sides hard to get it. To mediate is quieter and strictly neutral: whoever agrees to mediate helps the two sides settle their own quarrel without forcing any outcome.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

inflame: make a conflict worse

divide: drive people apart

Where it sits · what role the go-between plays — moderate → mediate → arbitrate

moderate vs. mediate: Moderate carries less power than mediate: a moderator only keeps a discussion orderly and polite, while a mediator wades into a real dispute and guides the two sides toward their own agreement.

arbitrate vs. mediate: Arbitrate carries more power than mediate: a mediator stands between two sides and helps them find their own agreement, while an arbitrator listens and then hands down a decision they must accept.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — medi-

root — medi-: middle (Latin medius)

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make, to act (Latin -atus)

Put it together

Put it together: Mediate is built on Latin medius, 'middle,' plus the verb ending -ate: 'to be in the middle.' A mediator plants themselves squarely between two quarreling parties -- in the middle, belonging to neither side.

Use the root in a new word: intermediate

Root Check

Word Choice

Mediate takes a dispute as its object or brings 'between' along: mediate a conflict, mediate between labor and management. The mediator must be neutral -- if you take a side, you are advocating, not mediating. And mind the spelling: meditate, with a T, means to reflect quietly alone.
